←Module 2: Google Drive: Organize and Share
Lesson · 20 min

Organizing Files and Folders

Build a folder system your coworkers can follow: create folders, move and rename files, star and color what matters, add shortcuts, and make copies.

By the end of this lesson you can

  • ✓Create folders and folders inside folders
  • ✓Move files by dragging them or with Organize › Move, and rename them
  • ✓Star files and color-code folders so the important ones stand out
  • ✓Add a shortcut to a file in a second folder, and make a copy when you need a separate file
  • ✓Name files so anyone can find them

Lesson Notes

Read through the key concepts before you try the challenge.

Folders the whole office can follow

On the job

You are cleaning up Parkview's My Drive.

Files for both buildings sit loose in My Drive, one is still called Untitled document, and nobody can find the laundry schedule. Denise wants a folder for each building with a Maintenance folder inside, files named so anyone can search for them, and the files you use every day easy to reach.

Your task: Organize the files into folders, rename them clearly, and mark the important ones.

  • Create a folder: open the place it should go, click New › New folder, type a name, and click Create.
  • Folders can hold folders: Elm Street Apartments › Maintenance › Boiler.
  • Rename a file or folder: right-click it › Rename, or select it and press F2. Inside an open file, click its name at the top left.
  • Name files with what, where, and which: Elm Street Laundry Schedule, Lease - Elm 3B - Jordan Smith. Avoid names like Untitled document, scan001, or final final.
Worked example

Naming the boiler notes

A file called Untitled document holds notes from the Elm Street boiler inspection.

  1. 1

    Right-click it › Rename and type Elm Street Boiler Notes.

    Search finds words in names. Untitled document tells nobody what is inside.

  2. 2

    Move it into Elm Street Apartments › Maintenance.

    A coworker who browses instead of searching finds it where they expect.

  3. 3

    Leave dates and version words out of the name.

    Drive keeps the modified date and the version history for you.

Result: A file anyone at Parkview can find by searching or by browsing.

🔑 Name files for the next person: what it is, plus the building or tenant it belongs to.

Moving files

  • Drag the file onto the folder in the list, or onto a folder on the left side, and let go.
  • Or right-click the file › Organize › Move, choose the folder, and click Move.
  • Select several files first with Ctrl+click (or Shift+click for a range) to move them together.
  • If you move a file into a shared folder, everyone who has access to that folder gets access to the file.

Place every card to check.
A file can live in only one folder. When it needs to show up in a second folder, add a shortcut instead of a copy, so there is still only one version to keep up to date.

Challenge

Apply what you've learned in this lesson.

Organize a corner of your own Drive.

  1. Create a folder named Job Search, and inside it two folders named Resumes and Cover Letters.
  2. Create or upload one file and move it into Resumes. Rename it Resume - your name.
  3. Star the Job Search folder and give it a color.
  4. Add a shortcut to your resume in the Cover Letters folder.
  5. Make a copy of the resume and name it Resume - your name - Practice.
Deliverable: Submit a screenshot of your Job Search folder showing the two folders, and one of the Resumes folder, to your instructor or course folder. No Google account? Complete the practice simulation and submit its results page.
